## Abstract

Cell--cell communication (CCC) coordinates cellular activities that vary dynamically across biological contexts.
Most computational tools infer CCC by aggregating cells into pre-defined types, obscuring the single-cell heterogeneity that distinguishes functional subpopulations.
Conversely, methods that preserve single-cell resolution disregard how communication is differentially regulated across multiple conditions.
To analyze multi-condition single-cell transcriptomic data without relying on cell-type labels, we developed CCC-RISE.
Built upon Reduction and Insight in Single-cell Exploration (RISE), CCC-RISE uses PARAFAC2-derived eigen-states to deconvolve communication into interpretable programs across conditions, sender cells, receiver cells, and ligand--receptor pairs, then maps programs back to the individual cells involved.
Applied to lung transplant and Crohn's disease cohorts, CCC-RISE identified distinct sender and receiver subpopulations within canonical cell types, revealed coordinated immune signaling mediated by co-varying ligand--receptor expression, and characterized a transitional spectrum of cells between hormone-secreting states.
In comparison, aggregate methods either missed these programs, decoupled their coordinated signaling, or attributed them to whole cell types broader than signaling subpopulations.
CCC-RISE thus resolves disease-relevant signaling subpopulations invisible to aggregate methods by analyzing multi-condition data with single-cell resolution.

- CCC-RISE analyzes cell--cell communication across conditions at single-cell resolution, without relying on pre-defined cell-type labels

- CCC-RISE deconvolves single-cell transcriptomic data into interpretable communication programs defined by conditions, sender cells, receiver cells, and ligand--receptor pairs

- Mapping programs back to individual cells reveals signaling subpopulations defined by unsupervised eigen-states rather than pre-defined cell types

- Communication programs identified by CCC-RISE are obscured by CCC-inference methods that rely on annotated cell types
